stem: Which of these is a **gaseous** fuel?

options.rationale: Charcoal is a solid fuel.
Paraffin is a liquid fuel.
Coal is a solid fuel.
LPG is stored as a liquid under pressure but burns as a gas.

explanation: LPG (liquefied petroleum gas: propane and butane) burns as a gas, so it is a gaseous fuel, like natural gas and biogas.

stem: Which of these is a **solid** fuel?

options.rationale: Diesel is a liquid fuel.
Biogas is a gaseous fuel.
Charcoal is a solid made from wood.
Petrol is a liquid fuel.

explanation: Solid fuels include firewood, charcoal, coal and coke. Diesel and petrol are liquids; biogas is a gas.

stem: Which fuel is **renewable**?

options.rationale: Coal is a fossil fuel; it took millions of years to form.
Biogas is made from animal and plant waste, which is produced all the time.
Diesel comes from crude oil, a fossil fuel.
Natural gas is a fossil fuel.

explanation: Biogas comes from the decay of dung and plant waste, which are constantly replaced, so it is renewable. Coal, diesel and natural gas are fossil fuels and cannot be replaced.

stem: True or false: coal is a renewable fuel because it was formed from plants.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: It is false. Coal took millions of years to form, so it cannot be replaced once used: it is non-renewable.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: coal is a fossil fuel; it formed over millions of years and is non-renewable.

explanation: Although coal formed from ancient plants, it took millions of years under heat and pressure. It cannot be replaced on a human timescale, so it is a non-renewable fossil fuel.

stem: Name the main flammable gas in biogas.

rejected.feedback: Biogas contains carbon dioxide, but it does not burn; the flammable gas is methane.
Butane is in LPG; biogas is mainly methane.

explanation: Biogas is mainly methane, CH₄ (the same gas as in natural gas), with some carbon dioxide.

stem: Which of these is **not** a property of a good fuel?

options.content: It releases a lot of energy per gram.
options.rationale: A high heating value is desirable.

options.content: It is easy and safe to store.
options.rationale: Safe storage is desirable.

options.content: It produces a lot of smoke when it burns.
options.rationale: Smoke is pollution and wasted fuel.

options.content: It burns at a steady, controllable rate.
options.rationale: Controllable burning is desirable.

explanation: A good fuel has a high heating value, is cheap, available, safe to store and transport, burns steadily and produces little smoke, ash or harmful gas.

stem: LPG is sold as a liquid in cylinders. Why is it classified as a **gaseous** fuel?

options.content: It is made from natural gas, so it is always classified as a gas.
options.rationale: LPG comes from crude oil refining and natural gas processing, but its source does not decide its state.

options.content: It is liquid only under pressure; it leaves the cylinder and burns as a gas.
options.rationale: Its normal state at room temperature and pressure is gas.

options.content: It becomes a gas only when the burner heats it above 100 °C.
options.rationale: LPG boils far below room temperature; it needs no heating to turn into a gas.

options.content: Fuels kept in pressurised metal cylinders are always classed as gases.
options.rationale: Classification is by the state of the fuel when it is used, not by its container.

explanation: Propane and butane are gases at room temperature. In the cylinder they are kept liquid by pressure, but when the valve opens they become gas and burn as a gas.
hints: Think about what comes out of the valve.

stem: Match each fuel with its correct description. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

right.content: solid; renewable if trees are replanted
liquid; made from a fossil fuel

explanation: Firewood: solid, renewable if replanted. Diesel: liquid from crude oil (fossil). Biogas: gas from waste (renewable). Coal: solid fossil fuel. Natural gas would be 'gas; fossil', but it is not in the list.
hints: Decide the state first, then whether it can be replaced.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Fuels formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals are called {{blank:a}} fuels. They are {{blank:b}}, because they cannot be replaced once they are used.

explanation: Coal, crude oil and natural gas are fossil fuels. They took millions of years to form, so they are non-renewable.

stem: Many rural families cook over open wood fires in kitchens with little ventilation. What is the main health risk?

options.content: The fire releases radiation that damages the skin.
options.rationale: Wood fires give out heat and light, not harmful radiation of this kind.

options.content: Smoke and fine particles damage the lungs and eyes.
options.rationale: Indoor smoke causes breathing illnesses.

options.content: Acid rain forms inside the kitchen.
options.rationale: Acid rain forms in clouds, not indoors.
Wood does not contain chlorine in significant amounts.

explanation: Wood smoke contains soot particles, carbon monoxide and other irritants. Breathing it every day causes lung diseases and sore eyes, so good ventilation, chimneys and cleaner fuels help.
hints: What do you see and smell around an open fire?

stem:
The table compares four cooking fuels.

| Fuel | Approximate heating value / kJ/g | Smoke when burning | Renewable? |
| --- | :---: | --- | --- |
| dry firewood | 16 | a lot | yes, if trees are replanted |
| charcoal | 30 | very little | yes, if trees are replanted |
| paraffin | 46 | some | no |
| LPG | 50 | none | no |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which fuel releases the most energy per gram?

options.rationale: 46 kJ/g is slightly lower than LPG.
30 kJ/g.
50 kJ/g, the highest in the table.
16 kJ/g, the lowest.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate how many times as much energy per gram is released by charcoal as by dry firewood. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** reasons why many town families prefer charcoal to firewood.

points.description: Charcoal releases more energy per gram (30 vs 16 kJ/g), so less has to be carried and bought
Charcoal produces very little smoke
Charcoal is lighter and easier to transport and store

parts.explanation: Charcoal releases nearly twice as much energy per gram, so less fuel is needed, and it burns with very little smoke; it is also light and easy to carry.

parts.label: (d)

points.description: It is non-renewable (a fossil fuel)
It can explode or catch fire if it leaks
It is expensive / the cylinders and stoves cost money / it is imported

parts.explanation: LPG is a non-renewable fossil fuel, it is explosive if it leaks, and it must be bought (and imported) along with the cylinder and stove.

explanation: LPG has the highest heating value (50 kJ/g). Charcoal releases 30 ÷ 16 ≈ 1.9 times as much energy per gram as firewood and burns with little smoke. LPG is clean but non-renewable, costly and dangerous if it leaks.
workedSolution:
1. (a) LPG, 50 kJ/g.
2. (b) 30 ÷ 16 = 1.875 ≈ 1.9.
3. (c) More energy per gram; little smoke; light.
4. (d) Non-renewable; explosive if leaking; costly.
hints: Divide the charcoal value by the firewood value.

stem: Large amounts of wood are cut in some districts to make charcoal for sale in the towns.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain how making charcoal can lead to deforestation.

points.description: Charcoal is made from wood (much more wood than the mass of charcoal produced), so many trees are cut down faster than they regrow

parts.explanation: A lot of wood is needed to make a small amount of charcoal, so trees are cut down faster than they can grow back.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe **two** effects of deforestation on the environment.

points.description: Soil erosion (no roots to hold the soil) / siltation of rivers and dams
Loss of habitats for animals and plants (loss of biodiversity)
Less carbon dioxide is absorbed by photosynthesis, adding to global warming
Changes to local rainfall and water supply / land becomes drier

parts.explanation: Without tree roots the soil is washed or blown away (soil erosion), silting rivers and dams; animals lose their habitats; and fewer trees remove carbon dioxide from the air.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** ways of reducing the amount of wood used for cooking.

points.description: Use energy-efficient stoves (e.g. enclosed or insulated stoves) and pot lids
Use alternative fuels such as biogas, LPG or solar cookers
Plant woodlots and replant trees that are cut down

parts.explanation: Use efficient enclosed stoves that need less wood, switch to biogas or solar cookers where possible, and plant woodlots so that wood is replaced.

explanation: Charcoal needs a lot of wood, so cutting for charcoal can remove trees faster than they regrow. Deforestation causes soil erosion and siltation, loss of habitats and less carbon dioxide absorbed. Efficient stoves, alternative fuels and replanting reduce the problem.
hints: Think about what tree roots and leaves do.

stem: Describe the properties of a good fuel. [5]

points.description: High heating value: releases a lot of energy per gram
Cheap and readily available
Easy and safe to store and transport
Ignites easily (suitable ignition temperature) and burns at a steady, controllable rate
Produces little smoke, ash or harmful gases (low pollution)
Low moisture content

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A good fuel releases a lot of energy per gram (a high heating value). It should be cheap and readily available, and easy and safe to store and transport. It should catch fire easily, but not so easily that it is dangerous, and then burn at a steady rate that can be controlled. It should produce little smoke, ash or harmful gases, and it should be dry, because moisture wastes energy.

explanation: Each separate property earns a mark: energy per gram, cost and availability, storage and transport, ignition and controllable burning, low pollution, low moisture.
hints: Think about energy, cost, safety, burning and pollution.

stem: Fuels must be used safely at home.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why paraffin should never be stored in empty cool-drink bottles.

points.description: Children may mistake it for a drink and swallow it, which is poisonous / dangerous

parts.explanation: A child could mistake the paraffin for a drink and swallow it, which is poisonous; paraffin should be kept in clearly labelled containers out of reach.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How should a gas cylinder connection be checked for a leak?

options.content: Hold a lit match near the joints.
options.rationale: A flame could ignite the leaking gas and cause an explosion.

options.content: Smell the cylinder from very close for a long time.
options.rationale: Breathing gas is unsafe; soapy water finds the leak.
This does not show where gas is escaping.

options.content: Brush soapy water on the joints and look for bubbles.
options.rationale: Bubbles show escaping gas safely.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why a charcoal brazier must not be used in a closed room.

points.description: With little oxygen, charcoal burns incompletely, producing carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide is toxic (and odourless): it stops the blood carrying oxygen, so people can die

parts.explanation: In a closed room the oxygen runs low, so the charcoal burns incompletely and makes carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas with no smell that stops the blood carrying oxygen.

explanation: Paraffin must be kept in labelled containers because it is poisonous if swallowed. Gas leaks are found safely with soapy water. Braziers in closed rooms produce carbon monoxide by incomplete combustion, which can kill.
hints: What forms when carbon burns in too little oxygen?

stem: Which of these is a **fossil** fuel?

options.rationale: Wood is renewable if trees are replanted.
Biogas is made from today's waste: renewable.
Ethanol from crops is renewable.
Formed over millions of years from plant remains.

explanation: Coal, crude oil and natural gas (and the fuels made from them) are fossil fuels. Wood, biogas and ethanol from crops are renewable.

stem: True or false: electricity is a fuel.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: It is false. Electricity is a form of energy; it is generated from fuels such as coal, or from falling water, wind or sunlight.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: electricity is energy carried by a current, not a substance that burns.

explanation: A fuel is a substance that releases energy when it burns. Electricity is not a substance: in Zimbabwe it is generated mainly by burning coal at Hwange and from water at Kariba.
hints: Is electricity a substance that burns?

stem: Which fuel is burnt at Hwange power station to generate electricity?

options.rationale: Hwange is a coal-mining area, and the power station burns its coal.
LPG is used mainly for cooking and heating.
Biogas is produced on a small scale from waste.
Charcoal is made from wood and used mainly for cooking.

explanation: Hwange thermal power station burns coal from the Hwange coalfield to boil water; the steam drives turbines that generate electricity.

stem: Which cooking fuel produces the least smoke and ash?

options.rationale: A gas that burns cleanly with a blue flame.
Wood fires are smoky and leave ash.
Coal produces smoke and a lot of ash.
Damp wood is especially smoky.

explanation: LPG is a gas that mixes well with air, so it burns completely with a clean blue flame, producing almost no smoke or ash.

stem:
A boarding school in rural Mashonaland must choose a fuel for its kitchen. It needs about 100 000 kJ of heat a day. The school keeps 40 cattle and there are woodlands nearby.

| Option | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| firewood | free from nearby woodland, but smoky; cooks must collect it |
| LPG (heating value 50 kJ/g) | clean, but must be bought and transported from town |
| biogas digester | costs money to build; uses cattle dung from the school farm |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of LPG, in kg, that would release 100 000 kJ. Assume all the energy is transferred.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which option is both renewable and makes use of a waste product?

options.rationale: Dung from the school farm would otherwise be wasted.
LPG is a fossil fuel.
Firewood is renewable only if trees are replanted, and it is not a waste product.
Biogas fits both descriptions.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Evaluate the three options and recommend one for the school, giving reasons.

points.description: Firewood: free and available, but smoky (health risk), causes deforestation and needs labour to collect
LPG: clean and high heating value, but non-renewable, costly to buy and transport, explosive if it leaks
Biogas: renewable, uses waste dung, clean-burning and the slurry is a fertiliser, but needs money to build and a steady supply of dung
A clear recommendation supported by comparing at least two options (e.g. biogas, with LPG as a back-up)

parts.explanation: Firewood is free but smoky, takes time to collect and contributes to deforestation. LPG is clean and convenient but is a costly, non-renewable fuel that must be transported and stored safely (about 2 kg a day). A biogas digester costs money to build, but it then uses free dung from the school's cattle, is renewable, burns cleanly and leaves slurry that can fertilise the school garden. I recommend biogas, with a small LPG supply as a back-up.

explanation: 100 000 kJ ÷ 50 kJ/g = 2000 g = 2 kg of LPG a day. A balanced evaluation weighs cost, availability, pollution, renewability and safety; biogas from the school's own dung is renewable and clean, though it needs an initial investment.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Mass = energy ÷ heating value = 100 000 ÷ 50 = 2000 g = 2 kg.
2. (b) Biogas: renewable and uses waste.
3. (c) Compare advantages and disadvantages, then recommend.
hints: Mass of fuel = energy needed ÷ heating value.
For 'evaluate', give advantages and disadvantages before recommending.

stem: Charcoal has a heating value of about 30 kJ/g. Calculate the energy released when 2.5 kg of charcoal burns completely, in MJ. (1 MJ = 1000 kJ)
